\section*{Executive summary and current status}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Executive summary and current status}

SCI-BEAM turns a Beammap observation into a scientifically traceable detector
property table. Its primary measurement is not an ideal optical beam. It is
the observation-local effective point-spread-function (PSF) core visible in
each standardized per-detector Beammap after that map's sampling,
pixelization, projection, gridding, filtering, finite boundary, and other
realized response. BEAM also measures the source amplitude in the raw detector
observable, derives relative focal-plane coordinates, calibrates each detector
to a fixed nominal-beam top-of-atmosphere convention, estimates an NEFD-like
sensitivity, and publishes the mandatory Beammap APT plus the empirical maps
and diagnostics needed to judge those summaries.

For one detector the physical input signal is
\begin{equation}
x_d(t)=\frac{\Delta f_d(t)}{f_d},
\label{eq:rationale-raw}
\end{equation}
the dimensionless fractional KID resonance-frequency shift. The fitted map
$x^{\rm BM}_{d,p}$ remains in $\Delta f/f$; \texttt{xs} denotes the
collection of these raw detector signals, never a calibrated
$\mathrm{mJy\,beam^{-1}}$ product.

\begin{table}[ht]\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}L{0.23\linewidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Input & Standardized detector-resolved Beammap in $\Delta f/f$, physical WCS/metric, valid support, covariance state, parent map-response lineage, calibrator/source model, fixed nominal beam, source atmosphere, and optional soft locator prior.\\
Output & Complete Beammap APT with raw/horizon coordinates, full effective-core tensor, amplitude, top-of-atmosphere nominal-beam \texttt{flxscale}, NEFD-like \texttt{sens}, independent quantity states, and immutable links to maps, residuals, covariance, and diagnostics.\\
Organizing fit & $x^{\rm BM}_{d,p}=A_d^{\rm obs}T(\boldsymbol\vartheta_p-\boldsymbol\mu_d;\boldsymbol\Sigma_{{\rm eff},d},\boldsymbol\phi)+\mathbf b_p^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta_d+r_{d,p}$.\\
Calibration & $\mathrm{flxscale}_d=F^{\rm TOA,nom}_{s,a}/(C^{\rm eff}_{s,a}A_d^{\rm obs})$, with no additional finite-source dilution factor.\\
Status & Scientific-owner draft v0.1/r0.2. Implementation, map-response fidelity, observational performance, science-impact qualification, and production readiness are not assessed.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\StatusBox{The contract separates validity by quantity. A valid effective-core
fit may coexist with unavailable \texttt{flxscale}; a valid calibration may
coexist with unavailable \texttt{sens}; a precise Gaussian core may coexist
with unknown wing power; and a useful telescope-health measurement need not be
qualified as a downstream kernel.}

\tableofcontents\clearpage

\section{What BEAM measures}
\label{sec:what}

A Beammap deliberately moves a bright source through a detector field so that
each detector obtains a spatial response measurement. SCI-BEAM v0.1 fits the
standardized detector map, not the detector timestream. The map is required to
remain in raw $\Delta f/f$ because the same observation supplies the evidence
from which detector calibration is derived. A map already calibrated to
$\mathrm{mJy\,beam^{-1}}$ would obscure or circularize that derivation.

The empirical per-detector map is the measurement. The fitted ellipse is a
compact model of its measurable high-signal-to-noise core. This distinction is
essential for an aberrated telescope. Broad or asymmetric power may lie below
the detector-map noise, beyond the mapped radius, or partly within a fitted
background. A numerically precise core does not prove that the complete PSF is
Gaussian, that its wings are absent, or that an intrinsic optical beam has
been recovered.

Four uses therefore remain separate:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Amplitude calibration} asks whether the reference-origin source
response is robust enough to support \texttt{flxscale}.
\item \textbf{Sensitivity} asks what off-source raw-signal noise corresponds
to in a top-of-atmosphere nominal-beam point-source convention.
\item \textbf{Telescope-health diagnosis} asks how the effective core and
residual response differ from the nominal expectation.
\item \textbf{Kernel qualification} asks whether a Gaussian or empirical
response is accurate enough for a named downstream scientific calculation.
\end{itemize}

Success for one use is not success for the others. A Beammap can be a valid
health diagnostic precisely because it shows a severely aberrated response.
Conversely, an apparently nominal core can still leave the complete response
poorly constrained.

\begin{figure}[ht]\centering
\flowbox{0.78in}{Raw detector signal\\$\Delta f/f$}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.78in}{Standardized\\detector Beammap}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.78in}{Effective-core fit\\+ empirical residual}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.78in}{APT row states\\+ dense companions}
\caption{The v0.1 measurement chain. The effective PSF core is conditioned on
the response embodied in the parent Beammap; the empirical map and residual
remain part of the scientific result.}
\label{fig:measurement}
\end{figure}

\section{Nominal beam and calibrator model}
\label{sec:nominal}

Calibration needs a stable reference that is not redefined by the very
Beammap being measured. For array $a$, the source model therefore supplies
$F^{\rm TOA,nom}_{s,a}$: the predicted calibrator amplitude at the top of the
atmosphere, in mJy per fixed versioned nominal beam, for the declared source,
epoch, passband, spectrum, finite-source convention, and source-reference
origin. The nominal beam is a calibration reference, not a claim about the
instantaneous telescope PSF.

The source-brightness shape $S$ is kept separate from the effective Gaussian
core $G$. It is non-negative, unit-integral, and centered by a declared zero
first moment. Their convolution is
\begin{equation}
H=S*G,
\qquad
T(\mathbf u)=\frac{H(\mathbf u)}{H(\mathbf0)},
\qquad T(\mathbf0)=1.
\label{eq:rationale-template}
\end{equation}
The fitted amplitude is consequently the modeled source excess at the
translated reference origin. For an asymmetric source that origin need not be
the profile maximum. This convention preserves the subtle and useful r0.1
finite-source treatment while making the calibration numerator explicit.

Crucially, $F^{\rm TOA,nom}_{s,a}$ is already the nominal-beam source
amplitude under the same reference-origin convention. It is not integrated
source flux and is not convolved again with the fitted effective PSF. There is
therefore no additional factor of $H(\mathbf0)$ in the calibration ratio. An
extra dilution factor would count the nominal-beam finite-source convention
twice.

\begin{figure}[ht]\centering
\flowbox{0.92in}{Source model +\\fixed nominal beam\\$\Downarrow$\\$F^{\rm TOA,nom}$}
\hspace{0.05in}
\flowbox{0.92in}{Effective-core fit\\$T(\mathbf0)=1$\\$\Downarrow$\\$A^{\rm obs}$}
\hspace{0.05in}
\flowbox{0.92in}{Source atmosphere\\$A^{\rm TOA-eq}=CA^{\rm obs}$}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.92in}{\texttt{flxscale}\\$F^{\rm TOA,nom}/A^{\rm TOA-eq}$\\no extra $H(0)$}
\caption{The amplitude convention. The fixed nominal-beam prediction and the
fitted map amplitude use the same source-reference origin. Finite-source
normalization is already embodied in the numerator.}
\label{fig:amplitude}
\end{figure}

\section{Per-detector Beammap fit}
\label{sec:fit}

The fit uses a metrically orthonormal angular tangent plane. A full WCS
transformation, or a validated local Jacobian, must establish the two angular
scales, signs, handedness, rotation, shear or cross terms, and the correct
azimuth metric. Raw $\Delta\mathrm{Az}$ and $\Delta\mathrm{El}$ are not
automatically a Euclidean plane. If a local linearization is used, its
reference location and error across the entire fit region are part of the
result.

The effective core is one symmetric positive-definite tensor,
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\rm eff}=
\mathbf R(\theta)
\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\rm maj}^2&0\\0&\sigma_{\rm min}^2\end{pmatrix}
\mathbf R(\theta)^\mathsf T.
\label{eq:rationale-tensor}
\end{equation}
All three independent shape degrees of freedom are fitted together. Separate
axis-aligned one-dimensional widths followed by a rotation estimate would not
be equivalent. At circularity the tensor and common width remain meaningful,
but an orientation does not.

Scientists commonly use
\begin{equation}
{\rm FWHM}_{\rm maj,min}=2\sqrt{2\ln2}\,\sigma_{\rm maj,min}.
\label{eq:rationale-fwhm}
\end{equation}
When the Gaussian interpretation is available, the fitted core has solid
angle $\Omega_G=2\pi\sigma_{\rm maj}\sigma_{\rm min}$. This is not promoted
to complete beam solid angle while material wings may be unmeasured.

The fit is joint. Its local model Jacobian contains derivatives with respect
to amplitude, centroid, all tensor degrees of freedom, background, and any
admitted source nuisance parameters. Its covariance must retain material
amplitude--width, centroid--shape, width--orientation, background--centroid,
source-size--beam-width, coordinate--shape, atmosphere--amplitude, and
calibrator--amplitude relationships. Independent one-parameter error bars do
not describe this problem. At circularity, uncertainty is expressed in an
invariant tensor basis rather than as an arbitrary angle error.

Support is part of the estimator. Cropping, a masked core, a disconnected
region, or a one-sided background can change which quantities are identifiable.
A successful optimizer cannot manufacture information absent from the map.
The complete empirical map, support, fitted model, residual, background, and
model-adequacy diagnostics are therefore preserved beside the compact APT
summary.

\section{Detector coordinates and LMT field rotation}
\label{sec:geometry}

SCI-BEAM produces two relative coordinate representations. The raw coordinate
$(x_t,y_t)_{\rm raw}$ comes from the fitted source centroid in the
observation-local Beammap tangent plane. The horizon coordinate $(x_t,y_t)$ is
the same detector geometry after derotation into the declared horizon-fixed
focal-plane frame. The effective angle for detector $d$ is derived from the
time and elevation support over which that detector's PSF was actually
measured, using the same weighting that constrains the fit. The PSF tensor is
rotated with the coordinate.

A single observation-average angle is acceptable only when its induced
coordinate and tensor error is negligible relative to the required accuracy.
Otherwise the transformation must preserve time dependence or a detector-
specific effective angle. Each detector records the effective angle, time and
elevation support, weighting rule, represented angle range, rotation-law
version, and uncertainty.

The APT origin and the physical field-rotation pivot are different concepts.
Relative detector coordinates are defined only up to a common translation;
there is no scientifically robust reference detector. BEAM records a
deterministic recentering rule, but that origin is a gauge choice, not a
boresight measurement.

Likewise, the physical point about which the LMT field rotates is not yet
established as telescope truth. The relation is affine rather than guaranteed
to be a pure rotation about a known boresight. A conventional pivot may be
used, but it is labeled conventional. Unknown pivot error appears principally
as an elevation-dependent common pointing term and, when detectors have
different effective angles, as smaller differential geometry uncertainty.
BEAM does not relabel its ensemble translation as telescope pointing error,
absolute array position, or a pointing-model correction.

This limitation makes one transfer rule essential: every pair of bracketing
pointing observations and the science observation receiving their correction
must use the same immutable APT coordinate realization and AST rotation
convention. Then arbitrary centering and conventional-pivot terms are treated
consistently and largely cancel. Changing APT origin or realization between
pointing and science is invalid unless a separately authorized coordinate
transform proves equivalence.

\section{Amplitude and top-of-atmosphere \texttt{flxscale}}
\label{sec:flxscale}

$A_d^{\rm obs}$ is measured on the source-observation plane. BEAM owns the
source-atmosphere correction used to place that amplitude on its
top-of-atmosphere-equivalent plane:
\begin{equation}
A_d^{\rm TOA-eq}=C^{\rm eff}_{s,a}A_d^{\rm obs},
\qquad
{\tt flxscale}_d=
\frac{F^{\rm TOA,nom}_{s,a}}{A_d^{\rm TOA-eq}}
=\frac{T^{\rm eff}_{s,a}F^{\rm TOA,nom}_{s,a}}{A_d^{\rm obs}}.
\label{eq:rationale-flxscale}
\end{equation}
The factor has unit
$\mathrm{mJy\,beam_{nom}^{-1}}/(\Delta f/f)$ and retains the physical identity
of the dimensionless detector observable. If the standardized map is already
on a properly documented TOA-equivalent raw-signal plane, that route may be
used instead; the route is always explicit.

The source atmosphere is applied exactly once in BEAM. SCI-CAL later applies
the target-observation atmosphere exactly once to target samples. The source
atmosphere is neither omitted from Beammap calibration nor repeated during
target calibration. Source-model, nominal-beam, atmosphere, and fitted-
amplitude uncertainties are often shared across detectors or arrays and must
retain their correlation scope.

BEAM owns the internal sequence from fitted amplitude to calibration candidate
to scientifically accepted source-APT \texttt{flxscale}. It does not await a
SCI-CAL promotion. TolProj may later associate detectors or apply an approved
child-APT transformation. SCI-CAL consumes the selected observation-specific
factor and applies it once.

\begin{figure}[ht]\centering
\flowbox{0.90in}{BEAM\\fit + source atmosphere\\source APT \texttt{flxscale}}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.90in}{TolProj\\target association\\approved child transform}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.90in}{SCI-CAL\\selected factor once\\target atmosphere once}
$\longrightarrow$
\flowbox{0.90in}{Science map\\declared response\\and calibration lineage}
\caption{Producer--transformer--consumer lineage. BEAM owns source calibration;
TolProj owns an approved relationship or transformation; SCI-CAL applies the
selected factor and the target atmosphere without reinterpreting either.}
\label{fig:lineage}
\end{figure}

\section{NEFD-like sensitivity}
\label{sec:sens}

The PSF fit is map-domain, but \texttt{sens} uses scan-domain data because it
is a time-normalized noise measurement. For each detector, the actual detector
trajectory identifies scans that do not pass within the declared source-
exclusion region. A declared scan-level statistic $n_{d,s}$ is computed from
each admitted off-source scan, placed on the same source-atmosphere convention
as the APT calibration, and robustly summarized:
\begin{equation}
n_d^{\rm off}=\operatorname{median}_{s\in\mathcal S_{d,\rm off}}
n_{d,s}^{\rm TOA-eq},
\qquad
{\tt sens}_d={\tt flxscale}_d\,n_d^{\rm off}.
\label{eq:rationale-sens}
\end{equation}
With the declared time normalization, \texttt{sens} has units
$\mathrm{mJy\,beam_{nom}^{-1}\sqrt{s}}$. It is a per-detector,
top-of-atmosphere, nominal-beam, NEFD-like point-source sensitivity.

The quantity has two legitimate uses: a rough relative-sensitivity input for
approximate weighting and a detector/array/system-health diagnostic. It is not
a signal calibration factor, total calibrated uncertainty, exact inverse
variance, empirical significance, or complete noise model. A weighting owner
may adopt a relation proportional to $1/{\tt sens}^2$, but owns normalization,
admission, covariance assumptions, and permitted claims.

The exact scan statistic is deliberately not invented in r0.2. Source-
exclusion radius, baseline treatment, time-frequency range or bandwidth,
robust or spectral estimator, correlated-noise treatment, minimum scan count,
exposure normalization, partial-scan policy, and uncertainty/repeatability
statistic require owner decisions and validation. Individual scan estimates
and their scatter remain available. Broad diffuse aberrated response may also
contaminate apparently off-source scans, so \texttt{sens} remains an effective
point-source/system measure rather than pure intrinsic detector noise.

\section{Aberration, adequacy, and broadening}
\label{sec:adequacy}

Relative to a compatible fixed nominal Gaussian tensor, BEAM may form
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\rm broad}=
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\rm eff}-\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\rm nom}.
\label{eq:rationale-broad}
\end{equation}
This is a telescope-health diagnostic. Its eigenvectors describe broadening,
not necessarily the major-axis orientation of the total effective PSF. A
literal Gaussian-smoothing interpretation requires the difference to be
positive semidefinite within uncertainty. An indefinite tensor is not clipped
into a plausible kernel; it can indicate noise, convention mismatch, or
failure of a nominal-plus-Gaussian-broadening model.

Model adequacy cannot be compressed into optimizer status. Quantitative
diagnostics must examine structured residuals, support dependence, peak
displacement, asymmetry, excess response outside the core, multiple peaks or
lobes, core-versus-wing completeness, and possible amplitude bias. Thresholds
will come from science-impact evidence, not from the Gaussian equations.

Array-, network-, or observation-level stacks are useful optional diagnostics
for common diffuse response below individual-detector sensitivity. They must
declare recentering, inclusion, weighting, normalization, coverage, detector
variation, covariance, and parent maps. They are neither required APT fields
nor prerequisites for per-detector core, \texttt{flxscale}, or \texttt{sens},
and they do not become kernels without separate qualification.

\section{Beammap APT and companion products}
\label{sec:apt}

The Beammap APT is a required SCI-BEAM output, not an optional convenience.
Its per-detector scientific content resolves stable identity; raw and horizon
coordinates plus coordinate covariance; effective angle; complete effective-
core tensor, FWHM, and orientation state; raw amplitude and uncertainty;
\texttt{flxscale}; \texttt{sens}; and independent availability, validity,
uncertainty, and cause state for every interpretation and use.

The tensor meaning is authoritative even if storage later chooses equivalent
major/minor/angle or independent-tensor fields. \texttt{responsivity} is not
part of the canonical scientific schema. Historical compatibility metadata
may carry the name, but its presence conveys no authority, its absence is not
an incomplete APT, and new production does not fabricate a value.

APT-level lineage resolves the observation, calibrator and epoch, source
model, fixed nominal beam, TOA amplitude convention, passband/spectrum, source
atmosphere, raw-signal definition/sign, WCS/Jacobian, field-rotation law,
conventional pivot status, common-origin rule, parent map response, PSF and
sensitivity estimator identities, contract/document versions, and immutable
parents.

Dense products need not be flattened into each row, but must be immutably
resolvable: empirical detector maps, support maps, residuals, full model
Jacobians, joint covariance, backgrounds, adequacy diagnostics, broadening and
wing constraints, off-source scan membership and statistics, convergence and
prior-route records, and complete QC/cause state. An APT without this required
lineage is not a complete SCI-BEAM result.

\begin{table}[ht]\centering\small
\caption{Examples of independent quantity state.}\label{tab:states}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}L{0.31\linewidth}YY@{}}
\toprule Situation & Still available & Unavailable or separately limited \\
\midrule
Source atmosphere missing & empirical map, core tensor, centroid, amplitude & \texttt{flxscale}; calibration uses \\
Off-source noise estimate fails & map fit and valid \texttt{flxscale} & \texttt{sens}; approximate weights \\
Precise Gaussian core, shallow field & core tensor/FWHM and health cue & wings, complete PSF, complete beam area \\
Indefinite broadening difference & effective tensor and residual evidence & literal Gaussian smoothing kernel \\
Aberrated but well-measured response & health diagnosis; possibly robust amplitude & nominal-science or kernel suitability pending impact study \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\section{Validation and open scientific decisions}
\label{sec:validation}

Different evidence answers different questions. Algebraic checks can establish
the identities, units, coordinate/tensor transformations, atmosphere
composition, and state logic in the formal contract. A later code audit and
tests can establish implementation conformance. Map-response, WCS, source,
atmosphere, and covariance checks are needed for representation fidelity.
Synthetic and observational campaigns are needed for bias, scatter,
uncertainty calibration, hidden wings, and repeatability. Downstream
science-impact studies are needed before kernel use, and production readiness
also needs owner-approved numerical policies and operations.

The PSF-recovery study must span nominal and broadened cores, rotated
ellipticity, arbitrary broadening orientation, asymmetric/aberrated profiles,
halos, sidelobes, shoulders, multiple scales, cropping/masking, varied S/N,
realistic map extent, correlated noise, backgrounds, and map-response states.
It measures bias/scatter in amplitude, centroid, tensor, FWHM, orientation,
broadening, residual diagnostics, and wing detectability.

A hidden-response study asks how much power can remain below noise, outside
the map, or absorbed by background, and how this biases amplitude,
\texttt{flxscale}, and \texttt{sens}. A kernel-impact study perturbs width,
ellipticity, orientation, centroid, circularization, model family, missing
wings, and Gaussian versus empirical response through the relevant downstream
science path. It must decide whether a Gaussian kernel is sufficient, a
regularized empirical kernel is needed, or no reliable kernel is justified.

Geometry validation includes WCS round trips, rotated ellipses, covariance
rotation, circular limits, Jacobian perturbations, broadening recovery, origin
gauge, conventional-pivot perturbations, detector-specific angle recovery,
pointing/science elevation separation, and exact same-APT transfer. This
rationale reports no result from any of these studies.

\begin{table}[ht]\centering\small
\caption{Uncertainty budget and typical correlation scope.}\label{tab:uncertainty}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}L{0.27\linewidth}L{0.24\linewidth}Y@{}}
\toprule Source & Typical scope & Required treatment \\
\midrule
Map noise/covariance & detector/pixel and map-process dependent & joint fit covariance or labeled approximation \\
Source size/shape & source, epoch, array/passband & joint source--beam propagation \\
WCS/Jacobian/rotation & observation, detector support, frame & coordinate--centroid--shape covariance \\
Nominal source amplitude & source, epoch, array & shared \texttt{flxscale} systematic/covariance \\
Source atmosphere & time/support, often array/observation shared & once-only BEAM propagation \\
Background/model mismatch & detector/support/model dependent & adequacy and amplitude-bias state, not only Hessian error \\
Off-source noise statistic & detector/scan plus correlated modes & retained scan values, scatter, and declared estimator \\
Conventional pivot & observation/elevation, partly common & common plus differential geometry uncertainty \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\DecisionBox{Sensitivity estimator and support}{The exact scan noise statistic,
source-exclusion radius, scan admission, exposure/bandwidth normalization,
correlated-noise treatment, and uncertainty statistic remain unresolved.}

\DecisionBox{Adequacy, wings, and kernels}{Evidence must determine diagnostic
thresholds, required PSF accuracy for each use, map depth/radius for wing
constraints, and the criteria for Gaussian, empirical, or unavailable kernels.}

\DecisionBox{Physical pivot registration}{A future authority must establish
the physical boresight and field-rotation pivot, acceptable conventional-pivot
residuals, uncertainty, epoch, and transfer domain.}
